newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish cabinet approves EU integration strategy.
newsitem.headline: Polish cabinet approves EU integration strategy.

text.p: The Polish government approved a programme on Tuesday for integration with the European Union, setting out further economic liberalisation needed for the country to join the bloc around the year 2000.
The National Integration Strategy said Poland would fully liberalise trade, the labour market, capital transactions and investment rules.
"I am very happy this programme has been adopted. Joining the EU is Poland's historic task," President Aleksander Kwasniewski told reporters after a cabinet meeting.

A dissenting vote was cast by Deputy Prime Minister Miroslaw Pietrewicz, whose Polish Peasant Party (PSL) is the junior coalition partner of the formerly communist Democratic Left Alliance. The PSL has adopted a cautious stance on EU membership.
The PSL fears adjusting to EU agriculture standards would be painful for Polish farmers and Pietrewicz argued the document lacked estimates on how much entry to the bloc would cost.

The EU says accession talks with Poland are likely to start in early 1998. Poland is seeking to join the bloc by the year 2000 and has won French and German support for this goal, but EU officials in Brussels say 2002 is a more realistic date.
Poland, along with the Czech Republic and Hungary, is widely seen as one of the first countries from the former Soviet bloc likely to join the EU.

But last year the European Commission, the EU's executive body, said that out of the three countries Poland had the most protectionist trade policies, which could have a negative impact on accession negotiations.
Since then Poland and the EU have sorted out differences over Warsaw's plans to protect its oil and steel industries longer than envisaged by the country's association treaty with the bloc.

However, Poland has yet to settle differences with the EU over car assembly regulations. Brussels criticised the terms under which South Korea's Daewoo. company was allowed to assemble its cars in Poland, saying they boiled down to duty-free car imports.

The goverment's programme for joining the EU, which is due to be sent to parliament for approval, also stated that in the longer term Poland would strive to join the bloc's economic and monetary union (EMU).

According to the programme, Poland would need EU financial help in the pre-accession period to restructure some ailing industries and might ask to be allowed to protect them longer than envisaged by the EU association treaty.
The government's European Integration Committee says agriculture and environment protection are areas in which adjustment to EU standards would last longest.
Analysts say Poland's steel, mining, shipbuilding, oil and other heavy industries are also far from being able to compete with Western counterparts without protection barriers.
The programme obliges the government to speedily adjust Poland's legal system to EU regulations.
It also provides for a broad education campaign about the European Union, aimed at preserving the bloc's favourable image among Poles.
Opinion polls show about 75 percent of Poles want their country to join the EU.
